title: The KKK: Loathsome Cosplay Rednecks
summary: Josh and Chuck trace the history of the Ku Klux Klan across its three iterations: the Reconstruction-era founding in Pulaski, Tennessee (1865-66) out of a fraternal-secret-society craze; its suppression by Attorney General Amos Akerman and the Enforcement Acts and Nathan Bedford Forrest's disbandment order; the 1915-1920s revival sparked by D. W. Griffith's film The Birth of a Nation and William J. Simmons's Stone Mountain cross burning, with its political power and up to millions of members; and the Civil Rights-era bombings (including the 1963 Birmingham church bombing), FBI COINTELPRO, and the group's decline into today's fractured, small remnants. They also cover the 1868 Louisiana election violence, the IRS tax action, local counter-protests, and a listener mail question from a young podcaster.

segments.title: Opening banter and personal connections to the Klan
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck open with personal reflections, including Josh's childhood in Stone Mountain, Georgia, and how his view of the Klan evolved. They frame the episode around the Klan's rise when America feels most racist and the fringe nature of its violence.

segments.title: Modern Klan documentary and origins in secret societies
segments.summary: They discuss a recent documentary on the modern Klan with scattered ideology, then the 1865 founding in Pulaski, Tennessee by Confederate veterans, drawing on the nineteenth-century secret society craze and the Golden Age of fraternalism.

segments.title: Name origins and shift to political terrorism after Reconstruction
segments.summary: The founders are listed, with the Sons of Malta as a possible influence. The Reconstruction Acts turned the group into a racist political terrorist organization, spreading across the South under Nathan Bedford Forrest. Theories on the name's origin (kuklos, Scottish clans) are discussed.

segments.title: Violence against Republicans and voters, 1868 election
segments.summary: The Klan targeted freed black citizens and Republicans who supported equal rights, with voter intimidation and murders, including about two hundred killings in Opelousas, Louisiana around the 1868 election. Fear-based recruitment is discussed, and the false balance fallacy is raised.

segments.title: Forrest's disbandment order and his later life
segments.summary: Forrest issued an order to disband within three years of founding. They discuss Forrest's role in the Fort Pillow massacre, his nickname the Wizard of the Saddle, his later speech supporting Black advancement, and controversies over naming honors such as a Jacksonville high school.

segments.title: Federal Enforcement Acts and Attorney General Amos Akerman
segments.summary: The federal government passed the Enforcement Acts in 1870 and Attorney General Amos Akerman used federal tools, including a prototype FBI and martial law in South Carolina, to break the first Klan. Membership estimates and declining numbers are noted.

segments.title: Ad break and Tom Petty tangent
segments.summary: Short ad break and a banter tangent about Gainesville music history.

segments.title: D. W. Griffith, The Birth of a Nation, and the second Klan
segments.summary: The Klan's iconic robes and hoods were popularized by Thomas Dixon Jr.'s novel and play The Klansmen and D. W. Griffith's film The Birth of a Nation. William J. Simmons was inspired by the film to revive the Klan with a Stone Mountain cross burning in 1915, with James Venable present.

segments.title: Second Klan political power and membership peak
segments.summary: The 1920s Klan expanded targets to Jews, Catholics, and communists and became a political force, with Senator Robert Byrd (a Klan member from West Virginia) and local officials. Membership estimated at up to four million, with strongholds such as Indiana. Local grievances and the Klan's mystique are discussed. The anti-Klan tactic of publishing membership lists is covered, and the IRS tax action in the 1940s is noted.

segments.title: Civil Rights era Klan bombings and FBI COINTELPRO
segments.summary: The third iteration's bombings, including the 1963 Birmingham church bombing that killed four girls, the Harry and Harriet Moore bombing, the Mississippi burning case, and Medgar Evers's assassination. FBI roles include COINTELPRO infiltration.

segments.title: Modern Klan decline, David Duke, and local counter-protests
segments.summary: The modern Klan has fractured and shrunk to under about thirty thousand members, with David Duke as a former Grand Wizard and House member. Local communities chased off a Klan rally in Madison, Indiana in 2019. The episode closes with a listener mail question and a baseball K-sign tangent.
